say: At the survival stage, money comes in and goes out the same day, and the owner is not sure whether she made a profit.

panel.heading: Which stage is your business in?

cards.d: Money comes in and goes out the same day. Business and household money are mixed. No records.
Fairly regular sales, costs written weekly, a separate purse, and the owner pays herself something.
Monthly profit known for at least 3 months, a cash reserve, and orders she has to refuse.

say: At the stable stage, sales are fairly regular, she knows her main costs, and the business pays her something every month.

panel.heading: Which stage is your business in?

say: At the growth-ready stage, demand is bigger than she can supply, and she has the records to prove it.
You cannot safely skip a level. A loan taken at survival stage usually feeds the household.

say: Each business has a main limit, and each limit needs a different fix. Demand means not enough people are buying.

panel.heading: What is really holding you back?
items: Demand: not enough people buying
Capacity: you cannot make or deliver more
Cash: you cannot buy inputs in advance
Time: you are the bottleneck for every task

say: Capacity means you cannot make or deliver more. That is Aisha. Customers already want more than one fryer can make.

say: Time means every task waits for you. The fix is delegation and routines.
If your profit per hour is lower than a helper would cost, the business is quietly using your free labour. That is not failure. It is information.

say: Next, find out who really buys. People are polite. If you ask whether they would buy, most say yes and never buy.

panel.heading: Ask about the past, not the future
left: Would you pay 1,500 naira for this?
right: The last time you used a laundry?
What did you spend on this last month?
Have you told anyone about us?

say: So ask about what they actually did recently. Past behaviour is the best evidence of future behaviour.

say: Talk to your best regular customers, customers who stopped buying, and people who buy from a competitor. Each group tells you something different.

say: Write notes the same day and tally the answers that repeat. Blessing, who runs a laundry in Port Harcourt, found 7 of 12 people said late return was their biggest frustration. Only 2 mentioned price.

say: Now put the whole business on one page with the Business Model Canvas. Circle the two weakest blocks.
Then score the ten readiness statements, from 0 for not true to 2 for fully true. Here are five of them.
Titi, who keeps hens near Ibadan, scored 11 out of 20. Her lowest areas were no customer profile and no cash reserve.
Under 8, fix records and separate money first. From 8 to 14, fix your two lowest items. 15 and above, you are probably ready to plan growth.

panel.heading: Score yourself honestly
items: Records kept for 3 months
Business money kept separate
Unit cost known per product
Customer profile written
Cash reserve for one month

say: Remember. Growth spent at survival stage leaks into the household. Profit is sales minus all costs, and dividing it by your hours shows if the business pays you fairly.
Name your main limit. Ask about what people did, and fix your two lowest scores.

panel.heading: What to keep from this module
items: Growth at survival stage leaks into the household
Profit is sales minus all costs; divide by your hours
Name your main limit: demand, capacity, cash or time
Ask what people did, not what they might do
Your readiness score shows your two urgent fixes

say: Collect one month of sales and costs, even if rough, and work out your profit per hour. Hold five discovery conversations. Then draw your canvas and score your readiness.
Keep them safe for the end of the course. Now continue with the lessons below.
